RISC-V Architecture

RISC-V is an open-standard instruction set architecture (ISA) based on the reduced instruction set computer (RISC) philosophy. It was started in 2001 at UC Berkeley (the "V" stands for version).

Key characteristics:

- Open standard: Defined by a free, open specification (no licensing fees), unlike ARM or x86. Anyone can implement, extend, or manufacture a RISC-V core without paying royalties.

- Modular base + extensions: The ISA is built in layers:
  * Base ISA: RV32I or RV64I (32- or 64-bit integer base)
  * Optional extensions:
    - M: Machine/integer arithmetic (mul, div)
    - A: Atomic operations (load-linked/store-conditional)
    - F/D: Single/Double-precision floating point
    - Q: Quad-precision (128-bit)
    - C: Compressed instructions (16-bit, smaller code size)
    - V: Vector extension (for SIMD)
    - Zba/Zbs: Bit-manipulation
    - P: Packed-SIMD (newer)
  * Profiles: A standardized bundle of extensions for specific use cases (e.g., "RV64GCV" = base + atomics + float + vector)

- Addressing: Base + offset addressing (e.g., load rd, offset(rs1)). Register offset form (e.g., load rd, offset(rs1)).

- Registers: 32 integer registers (x0-x31), x0 is hard-wired zero. Up to 32 FP registers (f0-f31) when F/D enabled. Up to 32 vector registers (v0-v31) when V enabled.

- Instruction encoding: Fixed 32-bit words (or 16-bit with C extension). Standard RISC format: opcode | rd | rs1 | rs2 | funct3 | funct7. This makes decoders simple.

- Privilege levels (machine state):
  * M-mode (Machine): Full access, used by firmware/BIOS
  * S-mode (Supervisor): OS kernel
  * U-mode (User): Applications
  Each mode has its own CSR (control and status registers) set.

- CSR (Control and Status Registers): 40-bit wide (in RV64), accessed via csrr/csrw instructions. Used for traps, memory protection (pmp), timers, performance counters.

- Exception/Interrupt handling: A single trap entry point per privilege level. An exception vector table (or vectored table for interrupts) holds handler addresses. The `mret`/`sret` instructions return from a trap.

- Memory model: Weakly ordered by default. The A extension provides ordering guarantees (lr/sc, amoswap, amoadd, etc.). Can be combined with fence instructions.

- Tooling: Fully supported by GCC and LLVM/Clang. Common simulators: Spike (ISA reference), QEMU. Common open cores: SiFive (various), PicoRV32 (tiny, FPGA), CVA6 (out-of-order, 64-bit), RISC-V GNU toolchain.

- Ecosystem: Used in microcontrollers (TinyChip, Esperlab), server CPUs (Tenstorrent, SiFive X25), GPUs, embedded, and growing in mobile (e.g., Allwinner). Linux and FreeRTOS run on it.

Philosophy:
- Load/store only (no data in ALU instructions)
- Fixed-width instructions (simple decode)
- Few, orthogonal instructions (small opcode space)
- Hardware simplicity: easy to verify, easy to implement in FPGA, low area/power

Why it matters:
- No royalty cost, no single vendor lock-in
- Extensible: you can add your own custom extensions for specific domains (AI, crypto, graphics)
- Open source: anyone can read the spec (free), modify it, and build a core
- Good for academic research, embedded, IoT, and increasingly datacenter

Limitations / trade-offs:
- Smaller binary-translation and software ecosystem than x86/ARM (improving fast)
- Vector extension (V) is powerful but complex; not all implementations support it
- Ecosystem fragmentation: many different extension combos, though profiles (RVA20, RVA22, RVB) are standardizing this
- No single dominant silicon vendor yet

In short: RISC-V is to processors what open source is to software — a shared, free, extensible foundation that many organizations can build on.
